title: N-Row — な に ぬ ね の

points.name: な
points.explanation: The syllable な combines 'n' with the vowel あ, producing a clear 'na' sound as in 'nah' or 'natural'. The Japanese 'n' in this row is formed the same way as English 'n' — tip of the tongue touches the ridge just behind your upper front teeth. な is a very common syllable, appearing in essential vocabulary like なか (inside), なつ (summer), and なに (what). It also functions as the informal sentence-ending particle that softens statements into gentle assertions or rhetorical questions.
rules: Japanese 'n' is formed the same way as English 'n' — no adjustment needed.
な can be a sentence-final particle adding a soft, assertive or questioning nuance.
Don't confuse な with ね — both end in vowels of similar shape, but な has a more complex structure.

points.name: に
points.explanation: The syllable に pairs 'n' with the vowel い, making a 'ni' sound like the beginning of 'need' or 'neat'. に is one of the most important particles in all of Japanese: it marks locations (at/in/on), destinations (to/toward), time references (at a specific time), and indirect objects (to/for someone). You will use に hundreds of times a day in Japanese. As a standalone word, に means 'two' — the native Japanese counting word for that number.
rules: Clean 'n' + bright 'ee' vowel — very natural for English speakers.
に is the location/destination/time particle — essential Japanese grammar.
に alone means 'two' in the native Japanese number system (ひとつ、ふたつ、みっつ... but に is the pure stem).

points.name: ぬ
points.explanation: The syllable ぬ pairs 'n' with the Japanese vowel う, making a 'nu' sound — remember that Japanese う uses flat, unrounded lips, so ぬ sounds different from English 'new' or 'knew'. ぬ is one of the less common hiragana syllables in modern Japanese vocabulary, but it's definitely worth knowing: it appears in いぬ (dog), ぬの (cloth/fabric), and the negative verb ending ぬ (an old-fashioned equivalent of ない meaning 'not'). The character ぬ has a distinctive looping shape that resembles its neighbor め — careful not to confuse the two.
rules: Flat, unrounded lips for the 'u' vowel — avoid the English 'nu' in 'knew'.
ぬ has a complex looping shape — take your time learning to write it.
Be careful not to confuse ぬ with め — they look similar but are different characters.

points.name: ね
points.explanation: The syllable ね pairs 'n' with the vowel え, producing a 'ne' sound as in 'net' or 'next'. ね is easy to pronounce and appears in lovely vocabulary like ねこ (cat) and ねつ (fever/heat). But ね also has a crucial grammatical role: as a sentence-final particle, ね is used to seek agreement or confirmation from the listener — it's the equivalent of adding 'right?', 'isn't it?', or 'you know?' to the end of a sentence. You'll hear ね constantly in everyday Japanese conversation, making it one of the most important syllables to know.
rules: Clean 'n' + pure 'eh' vowel — no glide, no nasalization.
ね as a sentence-final particle invites agreement: さむいね means 'It's cold, right?'
Don't confuse ね with わ or ぬ — all three have similar looping elements in their lower halves.

points.name: の
points.explanation: The syllable の pairs 'n' with the vowel お, making a 'no' sound as in 'note' or 'north'. の is arguably the most important particle in the Japanese language: it indicates possession and attribution — functioning roughly like English 'apostrophe-s' or 'of'. For example, わたしのほん means 'my book' (literally 'I's book'), and にほんのたべもの means 'food of Japan'. Every Japanese sentence you'll ever read likely contains の multiple times. It's also used as a sentence-final particle to add a soft explanatory or emotional nuance.
rules: Clean 'n' + 'oh' vowel — stop before gliding toward 'w'.
の is the possessive/attributive particle, equivalent to 'of' or apostrophe-s in English.
The character の is just a simple loop — one stroke going counterclockwise. Many people find it the easiest hiragana to write.

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this character make?
chapterPractice.explanation: の makes the 'no' sound. As a particle, の shows possession — like the English apostrophe-s. It's written as a single counterclockwise loop.
に makes the 'ni' sound (like 'need'). It's also the crucial location/destination particle in Japanese grammar.
いぬ (inu) means 'dog'. い (i) + ぬ (nu) = inu. One of the first animals most Japanese learners pick up!
ねこ (neko) means 'cat'. ね (ne) + こ (ko) = neko. The internet's favorite Japanese word.
